name: Anaerobic threshold
seoTitle: Anaerobic threshold Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Anaerobic threshold: work out anaerobic threshold from the age. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The anaerobic threshold calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports anaerobic threshold immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. It suits a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Anaerobic threshold calculator work?
sections.html:
The Anaerobic threshold calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports anaerobic threshold in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the formula type); then you type in the age.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in years.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as haskell & Fox formula, nes formula and tanaka, Monahan & Seals formula. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Anaerobic threshold calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Anaerobic threshold=187 − 17 ÷ 20 × age
Anaerobic threshold=(17 ÷ 18) × maximal anaerobic heart rate
Anaerobic threshold=(17 ÷ 16) × minimal anaerobic heart rate
Anaerobic threshold=3587 ÷ 20 − 68 ÷ 125 × age
Maximal anaerobic heart rate=(18 ÷ 17) × anaerobic threshold
Minimal anaerobic heart rate=(16 ÷ 17) × anaerobic threshold

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Age = 10 and Formula type set to Haskell & Fox formula. Working through the relationship above gives Anaerobic threshold = 179, Minimal anaerobic heart rate = 168 and Maximal anaerobic heart rate = 189.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Anaerobic threshold = 179, Minimal anaerobic heart rate = 168 and Maximal anaerobic heart rate = 189 should be roughly the size you expected from Age = 10 and Formula type set to Haskell & Fox formula.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Anaerobic threshold calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the age — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Anaerobic threshold calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns anaerobic threshold, derived from the age. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Anaerobic threshold calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Anaerobic threshold = 179. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Anaerobic threshold calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
